hints: Focus on what atomisation really means, making one mole of separate gaseous atoms from the element.
Remember sulfur does not exist as single S atoms, its standard state is solid $\text{S}_8$, so you must start from $\text{S}_8(\text{s})$.
Check how many moles of gaseous S atoms are made, it must be exactly one, so adjust the amount of $\text{S}_8$ to give just $1$ mol of $\text{S}(\text{g})$.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of atomisation**

Standard enthalpy of atomisation is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state.

Definition rule:
$$\text{element (standard state)} \rightarrow 1 \text{ mol } \text{X(g)}$$

**Identify the standard state of sulfur**

Sulfur is a solid at standard conditions and exists as $\text{S}_8$ molecules, not as single S atoms.

So the reactant must be:
$$\text{S}_8(\text{s})$$

**Fix the stoichiometry to make one atom**

The product must be exactly $1$ mol of $\text{S(g)}$. One $\text{S}_8$ gives $8$ S atoms, so we need only one-eighth of it.

Correct equation:
$$\frac{1}{8}\text{S}_8(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{S(g)}$$

options.A: This is correct. It starts from the standard state, $\text{S}_8(\text{s})$, and produces exactly 1 mol of $\text{S(g)}$, which matches the definition of standard enthalpy of atomisation.
options.B: This is false. It starts from $\text{S}_8(\text{g})$, but the standard state of sulfur is solid, not gas. This would miss out the enthalpy of sublimation.
options.C: This is false. Although it correctly uses $\text{S}_8(\text{s})$, it makes 8 mol of $\text{S(g)}$. Atomisation must form only 1 mol of gaseous atoms, so the enthalpy here would be 8 times too large.
options.D: This is false for two reasons. It uses the wrong starting state, $\text{S}_8(\text{g})$, and it forms 8 mol of $\text{S(g)}$ instead of 1 mol. It describes breaking S-S bonds in gaseous $\text{S}_8$ only.
